name: Continuously Compounded Return (Log Return)
description: Computes the continuously compounded (log) return between two prices as the natural logarithm of the ending-to-beginning price ratio, ln(P1/P0). Log returns are time-additive, so returns over successive periods simply sum.
notes: Prices must be positive. The result is a decimal fraction (multiply by 100 for percent) and is slightly smaller than the simple return for gains.

name: Effective Annual Rate (from Nominal)
description: Converts a nominal annual interest rate compounded n times per year into the effective annual rate, (1 + i/n)^n - 1. The EAR reflects the true yearly growth once intra-year compounding is included.
notes: Enter i as a decimal (0.06 for 6 percent), not a percentage. As n grows the EAR approaches e^i - 1 (continuous compounding); the result is a decimal.

name: Macaulay Duration (Level Coupon Bond)
description: Computes the Macaulay duration of a level-coupon bond, the weighted-average time to receive its cash flows, using a closed-form expression in the per-period yield, coupon rate, and number of periods. It measures the bond's effective maturity in periods.
notes: y and c are per-period rates as decimals, and n is the number of periods, so the answer is in periods, not years. The formula assumes a bond priced with level coupons.

name: Modified Duration (from Macaulay)
description: Converts Macaulay duration to modified duration by dividing by one plus the periodic yield, D/(1 + y/k). Modified duration approximates the percentage change in bond price for a one-unit change in yield.
notes: y is the annual yield as a decimal and k the number of coupon periods per year, so y/k is the per-period yield. The result estimates price sensitivity and shares D's time units.

name: Bond Convexity (Finite Difference)
description: Estimates bond convexity numerically from prices at a lower yield, a higher yield, and the current yield, (Pm + Pp - 2*P0)/(P0*dy^2). Convexity captures the curvature of the price-yield relationship that duration alone misses.
notes: Pm is the price if yield falls by dy and Pp if it rises by dy, using the same shift on both sides. dy is a decimal yield change; a larger dy reduces accuracy.

name: Effective Duration (Finite Difference)
description: Estimates effective duration numerically from bond prices after equal up and down yield shifts, (Pm - Pp)/(2*P0*dy). It measures the approximate percentage price change per unit change in yield, capturing embedded-option effects.
notes: Pm is the price if yield falls by dy and Pp if it rises by dy. dy is a decimal yield change; effective duration suits bonds with cash flows that change as yields move.

name: Yield to Maturity (Approximation Formula)
description: Approximates a bond's yield to maturity by combining the annual coupon with the amortized capital gain or loss over the average of face and current price, (C + (F - P)/n)/((F + P)/2). It gives a quick estimate without iterative solving.
notes: This is an approximation, not the exact IRR of the cash flows; it is least accurate for deep discounts or premiums. Enter C, F, and P in the same currency units.

name: Forward Price (Cost-of-Carry, Continuous)
description: Computes the no-arbitrage forward price under continuous compounding as the spot price grown at the net cost of carry, S*exp((r - q)*T). The risk-free rate raises it while the dividend or convenience yield lowers it.
notes: r and q are continuously compounded annual rates as decimals and T is in years. If q exceeds r the forward trades below spot (backwardation).

name: Futures Price (Discrete Carry)
description: Computes a futures price under discrete compounding by adding the present value of carrying costs to the spot price and compounding at the risk-free rate, (S + U)*(1 + r)^T. Storage and financing costs push the futures above spot.
notes: U is the present value of carrying costs in the same currency as S, and r is a per-period rate as a decimal with T in matching periods. Income yields would be subtracted instead.

name: Black-Scholes d1
description: Computes the d1 term of the Black-Scholes option model, (ln(S/K) + (r + sigma^2/2)*T)/(sigma*sqrt(T)). It is the standardized distance of the log spot-to-strike ratio, and N(d1) gives the option's delta for a call.
notes: r and sigma are annualized decimals and T is in years, all measured over the same horizon. This assumes no dividends; a dividend yield would subtract from the drift term.

name: Black-Scholes d2
description: Computes the d2 term of the Black-Scholes model as d1 minus sigma times the square root of time, d1 - sigma*sqrt(T). N(d2) is the risk-neutral probability that a call finishes in the money.
notes: Feed in the d1 already computed for the same option, with sigma as an annualized decimal and T in years. d2 is always less than d1 by the volatility term sigma*sqrt(T).

name: Put-Call Parity (Implied Call Value)
description: Uses put-call parity to derive the European call value from the put price, spot, and the present value of the strike, P + S - K*exp(-r*T). It enforces the no-arbitrage relationship linking calls, puts, and the underlying.
notes: Applies to European options on a non-dividend-paying asset with matching strike and expiry. r is a continuously compounded decimal rate and T is in years.

name: Black-Scholes Gamma
description: Computes the Black-Scholes gamma, the rate of change of option delta with respect to the spot price, exp(-d1^2/2)/(S*sigma*sqrt(2*pi*T)). Gamma peaks for at-the-money options and fades as expiry nears for others.
notes: Uses the standard normal density of d1. Gamma is identical for a call and its matching put; sigma is annualized and T is in years. Assumes no dividends.

name: Black-Scholes Vega
description: Computes the Black-Scholes vega, the sensitivity of option value to a change in volatility, S*exp(-d1^2/2)*sqrt(T)/sqrt(2*pi). It shows how much the option premium rises when implied volatility increases.
notes: Uses the standard normal density of d1. Vega is the same for a call and its matching put and is largest for at-the-money, longer-dated options. T is in years; assumes no dividends.

name: Sortino Ratio
description: Computes the Sortino ratio, the excess return over the risk-free rate per unit of downside deviation, (Rp - Rf)/dd. Unlike the Sharpe ratio it penalizes only harmful downside volatility, not upside swings.
notes: dd is the downside deviation (only below-target returns), not total standard deviation, and must be positive. Enter all returns as decimals over the same period.

name: Information Ratio
description: Computes the information ratio, the portfolio's active return over a benchmark divided by its tracking error, (Rp - Rb)/te. It measures the consistency of active-management skill per unit of active risk.
notes: te is the tracking error, the standard deviation of the return difference from the benchmark, and must be positive. Enter returns as decimals over the same horizon.

name: Beta (Covariance Method)
description: Computes an asset's beta as the covariance of its returns with the market divided by the market's variance, cov/varm. Beta measures how much the asset tends to move for a given market move; 1 means it tracks the market.
notes: cov and varm must be computed over the same return series and period. A beta above 1 signals higher systematic risk than the market, below 1 lower.

name: Capital Market Line (Expected Return)
description: Gives the expected return of an efficient portfolio on the capital market line, Rf + (Rm - Rf)/sm*sp. It adds the risk-free rate to the market price of risk times the portfolio's total standard deviation.
notes: The CML applies only to efficient portfolios and uses total risk (standard deviation), not beta. Enter rates and deviations as decimals; sm must be positive.

name: Preferred Stock Valuation
description: Values a preferred share as a perpetuity, dividing the fixed annual dividend by the required rate of return, D/r. It gives the present value of an unending stream of level dividends.
notes: Assumes a constant, perpetual dividend with no growth. r is the required return as a decimal and must be positive; the result is in the same currency as the dividend.

name: Internal Growth Rate
description: Computes the internal growth rate, the maximum rate a firm can grow using only retained earnings without external financing, ROA*b/(1 - ROA*b). It combines return on assets with the earnings retention ratio.
notes: ROA and b are decimals, with b the fraction of earnings retained (1 minus payout). The denominator must stay positive, so ROA*b must be less than 1.

name: EV/EBITDA Multiple
description: Computes the EV/EBITDA valuation multiple by dividing enterprise value by EBITDA, EV/EBITDA. It expresses company value relative to operating cash earnings, allowing comparison across firms with different capital structures.
notes: Both inputs must be in the same currency and period; the result is a multiple (x). It is capital-structure neutral, unlike the price-to-earnings ratio.

name: Free Cash Flow to Firm (FCFF)
description: Computes free cash flow to the firm from after-tax operating profit plus depreciation, less capital expenditure and the increase in working capital, EBIT*(1-t) + dep - capex - dwc. It is the cash available to all capital providers.
notes: t is the tax rate as a decimal, and dwc is the increase in net working capital (a decrease would add cash). All amounts should share the same currency and period.

name: Free Cash Flow to Equity (FCFE)
description: Derives free cash flow to equity from FCFF by subtracting after-tax interest expense and adding net borrowing, FCFF - intexp*(1-t) + nb. It is the cash available to equity holders after servicing debt.
notes: t is the tax rate as a decimal, and nb is net borrowing (new debt minus repayments); negative net borrowing reduces FCFE. Keep all figures in the same currency and period.

name: Terminal Value (Perpetuity Growth)
description: Computes the terminal value of a cash-flow stream using the Gordon growth model, the next-year cash flow divided by the discount rate less the growth rate, FCF*(1+g)/(r-g). It captures all value beyond the explicit forecast horizon.
notes: Requires r greater than g or the value becomes meaningless; g should be a modest long-run rate below the discount rate. FCF is the final explicit-year cash flow, grown one period.

name: Internal Rate of Return (Two-Cashflow Approximation)
description: Computes the annualized internal rate of return for a single investment and single payoff as the compound annual growth rate, (FV/PV)^(1/n) - 1. It is the constant yearly rate that grows the present value into the future value.
notes: Valid only for one outflow and one inflow, not for multiple interim cash flows. PV and FV must be positive and in the same currency; n is the number of years.

name: Continuous Compounding Discount Factor
description: Computes the present-value discount factor exp(-r*t) under continuous compounding, giving how much one unit of currency received at time t is worth today at continuous rate r. Multiply a future amount by this factor to discount it to the present.
notes: The rate r is a continuous (force of interest) decimal, not an annual percentage compounded discretely; time t is in years matching r. The factor is always between 0 and 1 for positive r and t.

name: Effective Annual Rate (Continuous Compounding)
description: Converts a nominal continuously compounded rate r into the equivalent effective annual rate exp(r)-1, the actual proportional growth of money over one year. This lets a continuous rate be compared with rates quoted on an annual basis.
notes: The result is a decimal fraction, so 0.05127 means about 5.127%. The effective rate always exceeds the nominal continuous rate because of continuous compounding.

name: Fisher Equation (Exact Nominal Rate)
description: Combines a real rate r and an inflation rate i into the exact nominal rate (1+r)(1+i)-1. It gives the interest rate needed to achieve real return r once inflation i erodes purchasing power, rather than the simple approximation r+i.
notes: Both r and i are decimal fractions (0.03 = 3%). The exact form adds a cross term r*i that the approximation r+i omits, so it differs noticeably at high rates.

name: Loan Amortization Payment
description: Computes the fixed periodic payment on a fully amortizing loan of principal P at rate r per period over n payments, using P*r/(1-(1+r)^(-n)). Each equal payment covers interest plus principal so the balance reaches zero after n periods.
notes: The rate r is per payment period, not annual, so divide an annual rate by the payments per year. All three inputs must use the same period; a monthly loan needs a monthly r and n counted in months.

name: Remaining Loan Balance
description: Gives the outstanding loan balance after k payments as the compounded original principal P*(1+r)^k minus the future value of the payments already made, PMT*(((1+r)^k-1)/r). The result is the principal still owed.
notes: The rate r is per period and k is the number of payments already made, both on the same schedule. PMT must be the actual periodic payment; a mismatched payment leaves a rounding residual in the balance.

name: Kelly Criterion (Optimal Bet Fraction)
description: Computes the Kelly fraction (b*p-(1-p))/b, the share of a bankroll to wager to maximize the long-run growth rate given win probability p and net odds b (profit per unit staked on a win). It balances edge against risk of loss.
notes: Odds b are net (b=1 means win one unit per unit staked, i.e. even money). A negative result means the bet has no edge and should not be taken; many practitioners bet a fraction of the Kelly value.

name: Kelly Fraction (Continuous Returns)
description: Gives the optimal fraction of wealth to allocate to a risky asset, (mu-r)/sigma^2, where mu is the asset's expected return, r the risk-free rate, and sigma its volatility. It maximizes long-run logarithmic growth of the portfolio.
notes: sigma is the standard deviation of returns and is squared in the denominator (the variance). All inputs should be over the same horizon; a value above 1 implies leverage beyond fully invested.

name: Value at Risk (Parametric, Normal)
description: Estimates parametric Value at Risk as V*(z*sigma-mu), the potential loss on a portfolio of value V over one period at a confidence level whose z-score is z, given return standard deviation sigma and mean mu. It reports the loss threshold that will not be exceeded at that confidence.
notes: Assumes returns are normally distributed; sigma and mu are per-period return decimals. A positive result is a loss magnitude; z (e.g. 1.645 for 95%) sets the confidence level.

name: Net Present Value (Single Cash Flow minus Initial Outlay)
description: Computes the net present value of a single future cash flow CF received after n periods, discounted at rate r, minus the initial outlay C0: CF/(1+r)^n - C0. A positive result means the investment adds value at that discount rate.
notes: The rate r is a per-period decimal and n counts periods matching it. C0 is entered as a positive number and subtracted; only one future cash flow is modeled here.

name: Payback Period (Even Cash Flows)
description: Computes the payback period C0/cf, the number of years needed to recover an initial investment C0 from a constant annual cash flow cf. It measures how quickly an outlay is recouped, ignoring the time value of money.
notes: Assumes equal cash flows each year; result is in years and may be fractional. It disregards discounting and any cash flows received after the payback point.

name: After-Tax Cost of Debt
description: Computes the after-tax cost of debt rd*(1-t), the effective interest cost to a firm after the tax deductibility of interest, where rd is the pre-tax rate and t the tax rate. It is a key input to the weighted average cost of capital.
notes: Both rd and t are decimal fractions (0.06 = 6%). The tax shield reduces the effective cost only where interest is deductible; the result is always below the pre-tax rate for positive t.

name: Annualized Holding Period Return
description: Converts a total holding period return HPR earned over n years into an equivalent annual compound rate, (1+HPR)^(1/n)-1. It answers what constant yearly return would produce the same cumulative growth.
notes: HPR is the whole-period return as a decimal (0.20 = 20% total, not per year). The result is the geometric annual rate, which is lower than simply dividing HPR by n.

name: Real Rate of Return (Exact)
description: Computes the exact real rate of return (1+rn)/(1+inf)-1, adjusting a nominal return rn for inflation inf to give the true gain in purchasing power. It is the precise form of the Fisher relation, not the approximation rn-inf.
notes: Both rn and inf are decimal fractions. The exact formula gives a slightly smaller value than rn-inf; the difference grows as inflation rises.

name: Present Value Interest Factor (PVIF)
description: Computes the present value interest factor 1/(1+r)^n, the present value of one unit of currency received n periods from now discounted at rate r. Multiply a single future amount by this factor to find its present value.
notes: The rate r is per period and n counts the same periods. The factor lies between 0 and 1 for positive r and n and falls as either grows.

name: Annuity Compound Factor (FVIFA)
description: Computes the future value interest factor of an annuity, ((1+r)^n-1)/r, the accumulated value of n end-of-period payments of one unit each, compounded at rate r. Multiply a level payment by this factor to get the annuity's future value.
notes: Assumes an ordinary annuity with payments at period end; r is per period. For payments at the start of each period (annuity due), multiply the result by (1+r).

name: Equivalent Annual Annuity
description: Converts a project's net present value NPV into an equivalent level annual cash flow, NPV*r/(1-(1+r)^(-n)), spread over its life of n years at discount rate r. It puts projects of different durations on a comparable per-year basis.
notes: The rate r is the annual discount rate as a decimal and n is the project life in years. It is the reverse of present-value of an annuity; use it to rank projects with unequal lives.
